newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian stocks take little cheer from U.S. rates.
newsitem.headline: Asian stocks take little cheer from U.S. rates.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's overnight decision to leave U.S. interest rates alone drew a mixed response from Asian stocks on Wednesday, although the region's bigger capitalisation exchanges were generally lower.

Tokyo and Bangkok were the day's biggest losers, while Taiwan and Jakarta posted the biggest gains. Elsewhere, Hong Kong, Seoul, Kuala Lumpur and Wellington closed lower, while Singapore, Sydney, Manila and Bombay posted gains.

Japanese stocks fell sharply in thin trade but the benchmark Nikkei average managed to hold above the key 20,000 level. The Nikkei 225 average ended down 320.43 points or 1.57 percent at 20,093.03, its lowest since March this year.
Brokers said the fall was triggered by speculative futures sales, adding that the feeble sentiment may linger for a while.
"Trading volume has been thin all day and it made stock prices volatile," said Masayuki Matsumoto, analyst at Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was led down by losses in the property sector as a lack of incentives prevented share prices from retaining some early gains. The index shed 49.35 points to 12,766.02 after rising to a session high of 12,942.63. Turnover was HK$6.29 billion.
Henry Lui, analyst at Mansion House Research, said investors were divided about the future course of interest rates.
ING Barings sales director James Osborn said while Wall Street stocks made gains overnight, "the bond market went the wrong way for equities".

Thai stocks closed at a 41-month low as mainly foreign investors sold on a belief that the market was unlikely to improve anytime soon. The SET index fell 13.41 points, or 1.55 percent, to 853.82 points. The index last closed below this level on June 11, 1993.
Brokers said investors sold because they did not believe that new Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan would be able to quickly turn around the tide for Thailand's slowing economy.

Jakarta shares ended higher on fresh buying but ended the day below earlier highs after profit-taking in many counters. Indonesia's composite index rose 5.65 points, or 0.91 percent, to close at 629.45 points after touching a high of 630.60.

Taiwan share prices extended early gains thanks to speculative late buying of construction and financial shares, brokers said. Taipei's index ended up 40.95 points or 0.60 percent at its intraday high of 6,896.52, but turnover was slim.
Brokers said the index was buoyed partly by reports that Morgan Stanley strategist Barton Biggs had recommended boosting holdings in Japan, non-Japan Asia and emerging markets.
In Seoul, buying of large cap and blue chip shares was not enough to drag the Korean stock market higher, and it closed lower for the sixth consecutive session.

The composite index provisionally ended down 1.96 points at 661.39. Brokers said that blue chips were boosted by talk that the finance ministry had asked pension funds to buy 300 billion won worth of shares by the end of the year.
Malaysia's KLSE index eased 1.94 points to 1,191.89 and New Zealand's Top 40 slipped 2.49 to 2,351.22.

Among the winners, Singapore's Straits Times index put on 19.26 points to 2,195.78, Australia's all ordinaries gained 7.9 to 2,323.7, and Bombay's BSE Sensex gained 13.86 points to a provisional 2,997.88 close.
Philippine share also closed higher, with Manila's composite index edging up 12.59 points to 3,105.8.

SIMEX Brent crude futures edged higher, supported by a firmer ACCESS market in the wake of API stock data. Feburary was last traded at US$23.78 per barrel, up eight cents from the London settlement on Tuesday.
Hong Kong gold ended higher at US$369.20/70 against New York's Tuesday close of $368.40/80 on buying from Japanese traders in Tokyo.
At 1144 GMT, the dollar was trading at 113.55/60 yen and 1.5512/22 marks.
